title: Functions
oneLiner: Defining and calling functions, parameters and return values, default and named arguments, returning tuples, scope, side effects, what a function can change, and a first look at recursion.
keyTakeaway: A function takes inputs, does one job and returns a result. Variables created inside it are local to each call. Passing a list passes a reference to the same list, so methods like Add or append change the caller's list, but assigning a new list to the parameter doesn't. Python evaluates default values once, so never use a list or dict as a default.
explanation:
A function is a named block of code you can run (call) from anywhere, as often as you like, with different inputs. Functions are how programs avoid repeating themselves and how big problems are split into small, testable pieces. In C#, functions always live inside a class and are called methods; Python has free-standing functions as well as methods.

The inputs listed in a function's definition are its parameters; the actual values supplied in a call are arguments. A function can send one value back to its caller with return. Both languages let parameters have default values, so callers can leave them out, and let callers name the arguments they pass, which makes calls with several settings readable. To hand back several values, return a tuple.

Scope is where a name is visible. Variables created inside a function are local: each call gets fresh ones and they disappear when it returns. A function that changes things outside itself (a global variable, a list it was given, a file) has side effects, which make code harder to follow and test. Knowing exactly what a function can and can't change about its arguments is one of the most useful things to get straight early.

Finally, a function can call itself. That's recursion, the basis of many algorithms on trees and nested data, covered step by step in the recursion lessons of Data Structures & Algorithms.
